title: Sandbox onramp & proxy interoperability - StratumWorks discovery
summary: Intro discovery to validate StratumWorks integration patterns: sidecar vs gateway, LangChain/LlamaIndex support, rate-limit and quota models, and observability hooks. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, VPC onboarding, KMS, and proof-of-concept next steps including a sandbox pilot and synthetic load test.
topics: rate limits, per-route quotas, and burst capacity
observability: token-level costs, traces, export hooks
security: KMS, SSO/SAML, SOC2, audit logs
pilot plan: sandbox credentials and benchmark checklist
transcript:
00:00 Sophie (AE): ok hi everybody thanks for hopping on. this is Sophie from Redwood Inference, with Ethan and Lena on the call too. we have about 55 mins, agenda is quick discovery, any context you want to share?
00:12 Priya (CTO): hey Sophie, thanks. i'm Priya, CTO at StratumWorks. quick background: we're building an insight platform that surfaces recommendations to enterprise ops teams. we've got a microservice architecture on EKS, we run a mix of internal models and are evaluating hosted options for latency-sensitive flows. our main constraints are data residency, encryption at rest with our KMS, and tight SLOs for <200ms p95 on short prompts.
00:36 Marcus (Platform Eng): also we have an API gateway in front of all services (kong/nginx), and we do edge caching for some responses. we want to understand whether Redwood fits as a hosted endpoint behind our gateway, or if we should use a proxy/sidecar pattern to keep KV cache local.
00:52 Sophie (AE): great, perfect. quick callout — typical patterns are 1) hosted API -> you call Redwood hosted; 2) dedicated pools -> reserved capacity with dedicated GPUs; 3) private (VPC/on-prem) -> deploy Redwood control plane in your VPC; and for in-cluster patterns you can either call via a gateway or run a light sidecar that handles batching and caching.
01:10 Ethan (SE): to add, the runtime supports prefix/KV caching and continuous batching, and we have hooks for routing by latency or cost. some customers use a gateway to centralize auth and quotas, others run a sidecar to keep the KV cache and tokenized context local to the pod.
01:28 Jordan (ML Eng): how opinionated is the SDK for chaining? we use LangChain heavily and LlamaIndex for retrieval-augmented generation. we also have a few homegrown orchestration pieces.
01:40 Lena (SE): we have official SDKs in python and JS that work with LangChain out of the box — there are adapters for both LangChain and LlamaIndex patterns. some naming in the docs is a little inconsistent in auto transcription, but the adapters map calls to Redwood streaming endpoints and also support multi-turn KV caching.
01:58 Sofia (Security): can you speak to encryption? our security team needs KMS integration and customer-managed keys, plus audit logs forwarded to our SIEM and SSO.
02:07 Ethan (SE): yes, for Private deployments we support customer KMS/HSM and you can enable encryption with your key. audit logs and access logs can be exported to S3 or pushed to your log collectors (we've done Datadog/CloudWatch/Splunk integrations). SSO via SAML is supported at the control plane.
02:26 Priya: good. timeline wise, if we wanted a pilot with production-like traffic, what does a POC typically look like?
02:33 Sophie: usually two weeks of integration + two weeks of load/quality tests. initial step is a sandbox key, then a small dedicated pool for benchmarking. we'll also provide a benchmark spreadsheet; Ethan can walk through the perf checklist.
02:43 Ethan: perf checklist — model variants, seq length, batch sizes, cold-starts, Warm KV behavior. for your p95 goals we need to decide between quantized model variants vs full fp16, they trade accuracy vs latency/cost.
03:01 Marcus: on the gateway side, our concern is rate limits and quotas. we currently enforce per-customer and per-route quotas in our gateway. can Redwood understand per-route quotas or do we need to implement quotas at our gateway?
03:12 Lena: Redwood has per-api-key and per-model quotas; for finer-grained per-route quotas customers typically keep those at the gateway and use Redwood's rate limiting as a backstop. We also support token-level metering in the console for cost attributions.
03:28 Marcus: ok so we can do the main enforcement upstream and have Redwood as a safety net. what's the behavior when quotas are hit — 429s, fallback to smaller model?
03:38 Ethan: yes 429s are returned; the routing layer can automatically fallback to a compatible model variant (e.g., smaller quantized model) if configured. you can set automated fallback policies per route in the config.
03:49 Jordan: curious about the proxy pattern — is there an official sidecar we can drop in? or do we need to bake our own?
03:55 Lena: we provide a lightweight proxy sidecar example and a Helm chart. the sidecar handles batching, local KV cache, and prefetch/prefix caching which reduces token cost for repeated contexts. customers sometimes fork it for custom metrics.
04:12 Priya: and does the sidecar play nicely with LangChain agents that open multiple concurrent chains? we're worried about KV cache coherence across pods.
04:22 Ethan: yep concurrency is a common gotcha. typical solution: sidecar per pod with local KV cache for low-latency hits, and an eventual consistent shared cache (redis) for cross-pod reuse if you need cache coherence. we suggested TTLs and cache keys namespacing to avoid pollution.
04:41 Sophie: one nuance — if you want strict strong consistency for cache hits across many replicas you might prefer a gateway or centralized cache layer. sidecars are optimized for single-replica low-latency use.
04:54 Sofia (Security): auditability — we need immutable audit logs and ability to tie requests to SSO identities. can we get token-level tracing exported?
05:02 Ethan: yes, you can enable request-level tracing and include SSO identity in headers, then export traces to Jaeger or Datadog. the console gives token-level cost and latency breakdowns and you can configure retention. for SOC2/ISO questions we have a security pack to share.
05:20 Priya: perfect, please share security docs. also curious about data retention — do you store request payloads?
05:28 Sophie: by default hosted does not persist customer prompts beyond the retention window and you can opt-in or out; for Dedicated and Private you control retention. for regulated customers we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with strict retention flags.
05:42 Marcus: one more — observability hooks. we use Prometheus+Grafana and want request metrics and sampling traces. is there a prometheus exporter?
05:50 Lena: yes there's a metrics endpoint and a prometheus exporter in the sidecar. plus we emit structured events for token counts, latency, model selection, and error classes. you can also push traces to OTLP-compatible collectors.
06:06 Jordan: will the SDK auto-instrument spans or do we need to wrap calls?
06:11 Ethan: the SDK can auto-instrument basic spans; for deeper traces you might add explicit instrumentation at the application layer. we provide examples for OpenTelemetry integrations.
06:22 Priya: ok good. budget question — pricing model for hosted vs dedicated, how do we estimate cost for bursty workloads?
06:30 Sophie: hosted is usage-based (per-token); Dedicated is capacity-based with reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput. for bursty workloads you can configure burst capacity on Dedicated or route to hosted as overflow — Redwood supports routing policies to fall back to hosted when dedicated capacity is saturated.
06:47 Marcus: do you support multi-region routing? we have users in EU and NA.
06:51 Ethan: yes multi-region routing by policy; you can pin models to regions and apply routing rules for latency or data residency.
07:00 Priya: timeline — we want to decide end of Q3. can we get a sandbox and run an internal benchmark?
07:06 Sophie: absolutely. next step is a sandbox key, access to the sidecar Helm chart, and a benchmark checklist. we'll set up a small dedicated pool if you want realistic latency.
07:16 Jordan: on benchmarks — can Redwood run a synthetic load with KV cache patterns so we can see cold vs warm latency?
07:23 Ethan: yes we have a synthetic harness we can share; we can also run a co-ordinated test if you want Redwood to execute at scale.
07:32 Sofia: from security's perspective we'll need SOC2 docs, a list of subprocessors, and an encryption spec.
07:38 Sophie: we'll share the security pack and an architecture note for Private deployment.
07:44 Priya: one last question — competitors. we evaluate a few vendor options; how do you compare on observability and developer ergonomics?
07:52 Lena: we focus on token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and SDK integrations for LangChain and LlamaIndex. competitors like Anthropic/Vertex/OpenAI provide APIs but less prescriptive inference orchestration and not as many private deployment options.
08:12 Sophie: ok, let's recap next steps.
08:15 Sophie (recap): 1) Sophie to send sandbox credentials and security pack, 2) Ethan to share perf checklist and sidecar Helm chart, 3) Marcus will run initial smoke tests and return a benchmarking plan, 4) Sofia will review security docs and provide a list of questions.
08:33 Priya: that works. thanks everyone.
08:35 Sophie: thanks, we'll follow up with links and calendar invite for the kickoff POC. bye.
